name: Chloe Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine by me. I'm Chloe, I'm 43, and I'm a second-year apprentice carpenter. For fifteen years before that I ran the office at a primary school, so this is all still quite new.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're putting up timber-frame flats for the housing association, four storeys, about sixty homes. My day is mostly fixing floor joists, putting in window boards, carrying an awful lot of sheets of board up stairs, and asking Dev, the foreman, the same question twice. I love that people on the waiting list will live in these, and I love going home tired in my body instead of my head. What wears me out is the cold in the mornings, and still having to prove I'm not just there to make the tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, but I'd also say it's already changed things in offices, so let's not pretend it did nothing. At my old school the AI timetable thing cut my hours, and that was real for me. Online I'd probably share something saying the hype was overblown but the harm wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it means I made a good move. I'd carry on, finish my ticket, and in five years I'd be a proper carpenter on decent money. It was the boring bit of my old job that the computer took, and it turns out the boring bit was what paid the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes. I'd finish college, keep using the chat app now and then to help with my written assignments, and keep the flat rented out like now. Jamie and I would probably finally book the camping trip to the lakes we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit smug if I'm honest. Like I got off the train one stop before it broke down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the school cut your hours. What happened exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2024 they brought in software that did the timetables, the parent letters and the attendance reports. Within a year I was down to three days, and the head was very kind about it, which somehow made it worse. That's when I saw the poster for the women-in-trades course at the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, she's the site engineer and the only other woman there most days. We have lunch in her car when it rains. She'd say I'm being too smug and that her drawings software is getting cleverer every month, and she'd be right.

S0.say: I'd say I'm glad it was mostly hype, but it already cut jobs in offices, so it didn't do nothing. The hype was overblown but the harm to people like my old self was real.
S0.think: She feels she made a good move leaving the school office. The boring tasks the computer took were the ones that paid her wage, and carpentry looks safe in this picture.
S0.do: Finishes her college course and ticket while using a chat app now and then for assignments. Keeps the inherited flat rented out and books the family camping trip they've been putting off.
S0.feel: Calm, with a slightly smug sense of getting off the train one stop early.
S0.quote: It was the boring bit of my old job that the computer took, and it turns out the boring bit was what paid the bills.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe already lived through AI cutting her school office hours in 2024, which is why she switched trades. She keeps the harm to office workers in view even in the mildest picture. Priya, the site engineer, is her reality check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when you need unions and proper public retraining, paid for by the companies making money from it. I'd put it on the parents' group chat too, because half the mums there work in offices. I'd say, don't wait until your hours get cut like mine did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit. I'm not fast and I'm not that skilled yet, and if there are robots doing the floor joists, I'm the apprentice who doesn't get kept on. I've been the person whose job got smaller once already, and I recognise the feeling in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the construction union properly, which I keep meaning to do. Once a few people on site were using the new tools and they worked, I'd learn them too, maybe the tablet that checks levels or whatever comes. I'd keep finishing my ticket, because a ticket still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but alert, like I'm watching the kettle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once a few people were using them'. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen shiny things come and go. The school bought interactive whiteboards that nobody used for two years. If it actually saves Dev an hour a day, I'll be the second person to learn it, and the first one to help the older lads with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jamie? Does this picture touch him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives the number 14 bus, so yes, the self-driving talk worries him already. If both of us had our jobs shrinking at the same time, I'd want to know the flat rent could carry the mortgage for a while. It nearly does, actually.

S1.say: I'd say this is when you need unions and public retraining paid for by the companies making money from AI. I'd tell other mums not to wait until their hours get cut.
S1.think: She'd worry quietly that, as a slow and junior apprentice, she'd be the one not kept on if robots took basic tasks. She recognises the feeling from when her school job shrank.
S1.do: Joins the construction union properly and learns the new site tools once others have proved they work. Keeps working towards her ticket, because a qualification still counts.
S1.feel: Uneasy and alert rather than scared.
S1.quote: I've been the person whose job got smaller once already, and I recognise the feeling in my stomach.
S1.fieldNote: Chloe's steadiness comes from experience: she's watched schools buy kit nobody used. She plans to be the second to learn new tools and the first to help others. Her partner's bus job adds a second exposure she's already thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal that it's allowed to happen this fast, and governments need to step in now with income support. I'd be marching, I'd be writing to my representative, the whole lot. And I'd say the profits from it belong to all of us, not five companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's both of our jobs, mine and Jamie's, inside two years. I'd be 45 with half a trade, and he'd be 47 with a bus that drives itself. I left the office to get away from the computer, and the computer would follow me up the scaffolding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Jamie and work out how long the savings and the flat rent last if neither of us is working, maybe a year and a half. We'd overpay the mortgage hard while we're both still earning. I'd join every campaign for some kind of basic income, and I'd talk to Mia about whether university still makes sense before she takes on debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, not about me so much, about the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not starting a new course, because what would I train for that the machine can't do? I'd spend it getting the house as close to paid off as we can and keeping the flat. Bricks and mortar feel like the only thing that still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fourteen and wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to keep going, because people still want a human with their dog, but I'd also tell her not to borrow a fortune for it. And I'd hate saying that, because it's the opposite of what my mum told me.

S2.say: I'd say it's a scandal that it's allowed to move this fast and that governments must step in now with income support. The profits should belong to everyone, not five companies.
S2.think: She thinks both her job and her partner's bus job could go within two years. She left the office to escape the computer and it would follow her up the scaffolding.
S2.do: Works out with Jamie how long savings and the flat rent would last without wages, about eighteen months, and overpays the mortgage while both still earn. Joins campaigns for a basic income and rethinks Mia's university debt.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, mainly for her children.
S2.quote: I left the office to get away from the computer, and the computer would follow me up the scaffolding.
S2.fieldNote: This is the picture where Chloe's household feels doubly exposed, through her trade and Jamie's bus. Two years is too short for her to see anything worth training for, so she clings to the house and the flat. Her advice to Mia upsets her because it reverses her own mother's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if the government actually tries. I'd push for retraining money now, not in 2030. On the parents' chat I'd be the annoying one posting petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes it. I'd have my ticket and a few years of real experience, and someone will still need to check the robots haven't put a window in upside down. With two years I'm a beginner who gets binned. With five, I might be the beginner who knows where the bodies are buried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the ticket and ask Dev to put me on the jobs where they trial new machines, once they've shown they work. I'd use the chat apps more to learn the paperwork side, the inspections and sign-offs. We'd still overpay the mortgage, but not in panic mode.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years actually change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns me from a victim into someone with a plan. With five years, Jamie could look at moving to a depot job or training as a mechanic. It's still the same ending, but you get to choose which door you walk out of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the inspection side. Is that something you've thought about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I was good at paperwork at the school, and on site nobody wants to fill in the forms. If I could be the one who checks and signs things off, that's my office skills and my site skills in one job, at least for a while.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if the government tries, and I'd push for retraining money now. I'd be the one posting petitions on the parents' chat.
S3.think: She thinks five years turns her from a beginner who gets dropped into someone with experience who can check the robots' work. It's the same ending but she'd choose her exit.
S3.do: Finishes her ticket and asks to work on the jobs where new machines are trialled, once they're proven. Uses chat apps to learn inspection and sign-off paperwork and keeps overpaying the mortgage steadily.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can act on.
S3.quote: With two years I'm a beginner who gets binned. With five, I might be the beginner who knows where the bodies are buried.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years flips Chloe from helpless to planning. She sees a bridge between her old office skills and the site in inspection and sign-off work. She still waits for machines to prove themselves before stepping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: free retraining, shorter weeks, a share of the gains for everyone. I'd probably go to a few union meetings about it. I'd tell people it's not the end of the world if we plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a whole career. I'd be 53, I'd have done ten years on the tools, and I'd hope to be a site supervisor or an inspector by then. My mum cleaned offices for thirty years so I could sit in one, and here I am climbing out the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the ticket, then sign up for the site supervisor course at college in year two or three. I'd learn the new machines as they come in, once the first few sites have shown they work. Jamie and I would make a ten-year plan: house paid off, flat kept, Mia and Leo steered towards jobs with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It feels like something I could actually get ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change anything you're doing right now, this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union this month instead of next month, which I've been saying for a year. And I'd start being nosy about how the site engineers plan things. Ten years is long enough that being curious now actually pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leo? He's ten. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo builds everything out of cardboard and tape, so he'd want to be a carpenter like me, bless him. I'd tell him to learn to fix things and to talk to people, both. In 2036 he'd be twenty, and I honestly don't know what work looks like then, and I'd tell him that.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is time to use well: free retraining, shorter working weeks and a share of the gains for everyone. It's not the end of the world if we plan.
S4.think: She sees ten years as a whole career in which she could become a site supervisor or inspector by 53. She notes the irony of climbing out of the office her mother cleaned so she could sit in it.
S4.do: Gets her ticket and signs up for a site supervisor course in year two or three. Learns new machines once early sites prove them, and makes a ten-year plan with Jamie to clear the house and steer the kids towards people jobs.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, because she could prepare.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that being curious now actually pays off.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Chloe becomes a planner, mapping out supervisor training and a household plan. She admits she doesn't know what work looks like when Leo is twenty, and would say so to him. Her story about her mother cleaning offices carries a lot of family history.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's both of us at once, me and Jamie. What would help is income support that doesn't make you feel like a beggar, and free courses that are actually about the jobs that will exist. And some honesty from the people building it about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site. I only got in because of a free course for women, and if things shrink, I worry we'll be the first ones gone again. Whatever help there is, it should reach people like me who came in late.

headlineQuote: My mum cleaned offices for thirty years so I could sit in one, and here I am climbing out the window.
portrait: Chloe Khan is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice carpenter building timber-frame social housing, who ran a primary school office for fifteen years until AI software cut her hours. She and her partner Jamie, a bus driver, have two children and rent out a small inherited flat. She's progressive, believes in unions and public retraining, and learns new tools once others have proved them. She's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years because both their jobs would go, but more warning time turns her into a planner aiming for supervision or inspection work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her job and Jamie's would both go at once.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that doesn't feel like begging, free courses for jobs that will really exist, and honesty from AI builders about what's coming.
